name: Dapagliflozin

lead: Dapagliflozin (Farxiga) is a prescription tablet that makes the kidneys pass excess glucose in urine. It is approved for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.

People interested in leaning out note that it produces modest weight loss; in a large type 2 diabetes outcome trial, average body weight fell by roughly 2 kg over 48 months, and a kidney-disease trial recorded about 1.5 kg over short treatment periods.

paras: It is taken orally once daily under a prescriber for its approved conditions. Its use for weight or appearance is off-label and discussed in forums as a possible add-on to other fat-loss tools; no practical protocol is given here.

Common effects include genital and urinary tract infections; ketoacidosis (including euglycemic), dehydration and low blood pressure are recognized risks, and Fournier gangrene is rare. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU, Canada and Australia.

chain: Calorie loss and modest weight reduction
angle.text: Dapagliflozin lowers body weight by a small amount as a side effect of its glucose-lowering action. Forum interest treats it as a possible adjunct to diet-based fat loss.

lead: Dapagliflozin, sold as Farxiga and Forxiga, is an SGLT2 inhibitor: it blocks the kidney transporter that reabsorbs most filtered glucose so glucose leaves in the urine.[1] It is prescription-only.[1]

Approved for type 2 diabetes in the EU (2012) and US (2014), it was later cleared for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (US, 2020), chronic kidney disease (2021) and wider heart failure (EU, 2023).[1]

For appearance, interest centers on weight reduction. Glucose loss in urine removes calories, and trials report average losses of about 1.5 to 2 kg.[1] A 2025 systematic review lists dapagliflozin among agents in ongoing phase 3 obesity trials.[2]

paras: Dapagliflozin improves glycemic control in type 2 diabetes and reduces kidney decline, kidney failure and cardiovascular death in chronic kidney disease and heart failure, with benefits seen with or without diabetes.[1] The DAPA-CKD trial randomized 4,304 participants with chronic kidney disease, and DAPA-HF tested it in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.[3][4]

Wikipedia cites about 1.5 kg of weight loss in the DIAMOND trial in non-diabetic kidney disease.[1] Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, reports about 2 kg over 48 months in the DECLARE-TIMI 58 outcome trial.[5][6] These are modest averages in patients with diabetes or kidney disease, not people seeking cosmetic fat loss.

Genital and urinary tract infections are common because glucose in urine promotes microbial growth, and Fournier gangrene is rare.[1] Diabetic ketoacidosis, including the euglycemic form, is a known risk, and the FDA recommends stopping the drug at least three days before scheduled surgery.[1] Dehydration, low blood pressure and, with insulin, low blood sugar also occur.[1]

Developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb with AstraZeneca, first synthesis patented 2002; it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] Generics were approved in the EU (2023), Canada (2023) and the US (2022).[1]

Large randomized trials cover heart failure, chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes outcomes.[3][4][7][8] None of those trials targeted cosmetic weight loss in otherwise healthy people. A 2025 systematic review of emerging obesity drugs includes dapagliflozin in ongoing phase 3 work.[2]

timeline.event: US expansion to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.[1]
